out: Identify data types, states and classifications.
Pick a protection method to fit the need.
plain: Think of money. In a vault it is at rest. In an armored truck it is in transit. On the counter while a teller counts it, it is in use. Each state needs its own protection.
tech: Structured data has a defined format, such as database tables. Unstructured data has none, such as documents, images and email. Data at rest is stored. Data in transit moves across a network. Data in use is being processed in memory, which is hardest to protect. Classifications include public, sensitive, confidential, restricted, critical, and in government settings secret and top secret.

Methods: masking hides part of a value, such as showing only the last four digits. Hashing creates a one-way digest. Filtering removes or blocks certain data. Tokenization replaces a sensitive value with a random token, stored in a separate vault. Encryption transforms data so that a key is required. Data transpose rearranges characters or fields, a weak method by itself. De-identification (deidentification) removes information that links data to a person. Obfuscation makes data harder to interpret without strong protection.
terms: Data with a defined format such as tables.
Data with no fixed format, such as documents.
A government classification for serious harm if disclosed.
Data essential to operating the organization.
Data that can be shared freely.
Data limited to a named group.
Removing or blocking data based on rules.
Replacing sensitive data with a random stand-in.
Transforming data so that only a key can reverse it.
Removing details that link data to a person.
eg: A store's point-of-sale system handles tokens, so a breach of that system does not expose actual card numbers.
A support agent sees only the last four digits of a card, through masking.

walks.title: Choose a method
steps: Need to process payments without storing cards? Tokenization.
Need staff to confirm a customer without seeing everything? Masking.
Need to store passwords? Salted hashing.
Need to send a file securely? Encryption.
Need to share data for research? De-identification.

labs.title: Classify and protect sample data
do: Make a table of ten fictional data items such as names, card numbers, press releases.
Label each by type, state and classification.
Choose a protection method for each.
Apply masking in the spreadsheet for one column.
labs.expect: A completed table with reasons for each choice.
labs.explain: Different data needs different handling. Protecting all data the same way is either wasteful or inadequate.
pass: Each item has a type, classification and method.
You applied masking to at least one column.

qs.s: Data stored on a backup drive is in which state?

a.w: That is a protection method, not a state.

a.t: A sensitive value is replaced by a random stand-in mapped in a secure vault
a.w: The token has no mathematical link to the value.

a.t: A value is transformed with a key
A value is converted into a one-way digest
Only part of a value is displayed

qs.s: Match each need to a method.
pairs: Show only the last four digits
Replace a card number with a random value
Remove names from a research data set
Protect a file with a key
qs.why: Each method solves a different problem.

qs.s: Why is data in use typically hardest to protect?

a.t: It must be in readable form in memory while being processed
a.w: Decrypted data is exposed during processing.

a.t: It is always stored on tape
It is never present on endpoints

mistakes: Calling tokenization encryption. Tokens have no key relationship with the value.
Treating obfuscation or transposition as strong protection.
sum: Know the type, state and classification of your data.
Masking, tokenization, hashing and encryption solve different problems.
cards: At rest, in transit and in use.
How does tokenization differ from encryption?
A token is a random stand-in held in a vault, with no key that can reverse it.
lessons.title: Protecting data: types, states, classifications and methods
lessons.why: Data is usually what attackers are after. Knowing what you have and what state it is in determines how to protect it.
lessons.scenario: A retailer wants to keep customer card references for repeat purchases without keeping card numbers on its own systems. Which method fits?
lessons.answer: Tokenization. The retailer stores tokens, and the real numbers remain in the payment provider's secure vault.

product: Data classification decides what a person sees. Masking shows a card's last four digits, tokenization lets staff work with a stand-in, and reveal-on-demand controls record who viewed a value. The three data states also appear in product questions: is it safe at rest, in transit and on screen while in use?

eng: Is this field encrypted, hashed, tokenized or masked, and where does that happen?
Can a masked value be recovered by an API call that bypasses the interface?
sec: How is this data classified, and which rules follow from that?
prod: Who truly needs to see the full value, and how often?

ex.title: Design sensitive data display and access
ex.scenario: Staff at a health insurer use an internal portal showing member records, including government ID numbers, diagnoses and bank details. Today, every staff member sees everything.
ex.problem: Access is all-or-nothing, and there is no record of who viewed which sensitive field.
tasks: Classify each field on the record and justify each level.
Choose masking, tokenization or restricted reveal for each field.
Design reveal-with-reason, including the record it creates.
Design what appears in exports, printouts, logs and support screenshots.
constraints: Masking must be applied by the server, so the full value does not reach an unauthorized browser.
Hashing can't be reversed, so a value that must be displayed can't be stored only as a hash.
Viewing data on screen is the "in use" state, and encryption at rest doesn't protect it.
needs: Claims staff need full values occasionally, for a defined reason.
Members expect their data to be seen only by those who need it.
Privacy officers need to audit unusual access.
ex.deliver: A field classification table, a protection method per field and designs for the reveal flow.

crit.t: Each protection method is technically appropriate for how that field is used.
Exports, logs and screenshots are treated as leak paths.
Routine tasks can be finished without revealing unneeded data.
Reveal friction is matched to data classification, and it is not the same everywhere.

seniors: Masking in the interface alone is decoration, so confirm where the protection is really applied.
Classification belongs to the data owner, so use the organization's scheme and do not invent your own.

cq.s: Staff must verify a member's ID by comparing its last four digits and never need the full value. Which approach fits?

a.t: Server-side masking that returns only the last four digits
a.w: The full value never reaches the browser, and the task still works.

a.t: Client-side masking with the full value sent to the page
a.w: The full value is exposed to anyone who inspects the response.

a.t: Hashing the value, then displaying the entire hash to staff
a.w: A hash can't be compared by eye with what a member says.

a.t: Encrypting at rest and showing the full value to all staff
a.w: Encryption at rest does not limit who can view it on screen.

out: Apply marking, geofencing and placement rules.
Follow data through its life cycle and link it to compliance needs.
plain: A library has an owner who sets the rules, a librarian who looks after the books and an assistant who checks them out. Data has similar roles. Data also has a life, from being created until it is securely destroyed.
tech: Data protection roles: the data owner is accountable for the data and decides how it is classified. The data custodian implements and maintains the technical controls. The data steward looks after data quality and proper use. The data operator handles day-to-day processing. The data controller decides why and how personal data is processed. A data subprocessor is engaged by a processor to carry out part of the processing.

Data handling covers: endpoints, where data is often copied and lost; marking and labeling, which show classification; geofencing, which restricts access by location; data location, where data physically resides; and data placement, deciding where data is stored according to its sensitivity.

The data management life cycle covers creation, management, distribution, retention and disposal. Data compliance is shaped by standards and by the kind of data: health data, personal information, financial data, child/minor data, intellectual property and legal data. Examples include HIPAA for US health data, GDPR in the EU and PIPEDA in Canada, and PCI DSS for payment card data.
terms: The person accountable for a set of data.
The role responsible for data quality and proper use.
The role carrying out day-to-day data handling.
The party deciding why and how personal data is processed.
A company engaged by a processor to help process data.
Laptops, phones and desktops where data is handled.
Showing data's classification on or within it.
Choosing where to store data based on sensitivity and rules.
The stage in which data begins to exist.
Sharing data with those who need it.
Keeping data for a defined period.
Data relating to an identifiable person.
Data such as card and bank information.
Information about children, with extra protections.
eg: A hospital (controller) uses a billing company (processor), which uses a cloud host as a subprocessor. Contracts must cover each of these relationships.
A company allows access to a finance app only from Canada, using geofencing.

walks.title: Follow a customer record through the life cycle
steps: Creation: a customer signs up, and the record is classified.
Management: staff update it under access controls.
Distribution: a shipping partner receives only the address.
Retention: it is kept for the legally required period.
Disposal: it is securely deleted at the end of the period.

labs.title: Draw a data flow
labs.tool: Drawing tool and PIPEDA or GDPR summary
do: Pick a fictional online shop. Draw where customer data is created, stored and shared.
Label the controller, processor and any subprocessors.
Note one obligation from PIPEDA or GDPR that applies.
labs.expect: A diagram with roles and life-cycle points marked.
labs.explain: A map like this is what privacy teams need before answering a regulator or a data subject.
pass: Every life-cycle stage appears in your diagram.

qs.s: Who is accountable for classifying a data set?

a.w: Auditors assess, and do not own.

qs.s: A retailer decides what customer data to collect and why, and a payroll vendor processes it as directed. What is the retailer?

a.w: It determines the purpose and means.
That is a further third party.

qs.s: Put the stages of the data life cycle in order.
qs.why: Data must be created and managed before it is distributed, and retained before it is disposed of.

qs.s: A company blocks sign-ins from outside its operating region. What technique is this?

mistakes: Confusing owner and custodian. The owner is accountable, while the custodian operates the controls.
Keeping data indefinitely, since unneeded data is liability.
sum: Handling rules apply on endpoints and in storage.
Data has a life cycle, ending with secure disposal.
cards: What is the difference between a data owner and a data custodian?
The owner is accountable, and the custodian implements the protection.
Name the five data life-cycle stages.
lessons.title: Data roles, handling, life cycle and compliance
lessons.why: When everyone is responsible, no one is. Clearly assigned data roles and known life-cycle stages are the backbone of privacy obligations.
lessons.scenario: A database administrator applies encryption and access controls according to rules set by a business leader, who is accountable for the data. Which roles are these?
lessons.answer: The database administrator is the data custodian, and the business leader is the data owner.

product: Data subject rights become product flows: download my data, delete my account, correct this record. Deletion is especially tricky because data lives in backups, logs and third-party tools. Retention rules or legal holds can also require the opposite of what the user asks.

eng: Where does this person's data live, including backups and third parties?
How long until deletion is actually complete everywhere?
sec: How do we verify the identity of the person requesting an export?
prod: What are our legal retention obligations, and who confirms them?

ex.title: Design data export and deletion
ex.scenario: A B2B product with customers in the EU receives requests from individual users to export and delete their data. The customer organization is the data controller, and it also has retention rules.
ex.problem: Requests are handled by email and spreadsheets, with no verification, unclear ownership and no way to say what was deleted.
tasks: Map the data roles: controller, processor, owner and custodian for this product.
Design the request, verification, approval and progress flow.
Design the export package experience, including secure delivery and expiry.
Write honest messages for partial deletion, retention holds and backup timing.
constraints: An export is a concentrated copy of sensitive data, so it needs strong verification and expiry.
A legal hold can override a deletion request.
The customer organization may need to approve or be told about requests.
needs: Individuals need to know what happened to their data, and when.
Customer administrators need to meet their own obligations.
Legal and privacy staff need a defensible record.
ex.deliver: A flow from request to confirmation, an export delivery design and a set of status messages.

crit.t: The flow respects controller and processor roles and legal holds.
An attacker requesting an export is treated as a real scenario.
Status messages are specific about what is done, what is pending and why.
The design is reviewed against actual legal requirements through named stakeholders.

seniors: You are not giving legal advice, so bring questions to privacy counsel and let them confirm the requirement.
Deletion that can't be verified should not be described as complete.

cq.s: A user requests deletion, but a legal hold applies to some records. What should the product say?

a.t: What was deleted, what remains and why it remains
a.w: Honest specifics respect the user and the legal obligation.

a.t: All of your data has now been permanently deleted
a.w: This would be false, and it could create legal exposure.

a.t: Your request failed, so please try again next month
a.w: The request did not fail, and the user learns nothing.

a.t: Nothing, because legal holds are confidential processes
a.w: The hold's details may be limited, but the outcome should still be communicated.

out: Compare hot, warm and cold sites.
plain: A hot site is a furnished, stocked spare office you can walk into right away. A warm site has furniture but needs setup. A cold site is an empty room with power and a lease. Redundancy is keeping a spare tire, and load balancing is sharing the weight among several tires.
tech: Site considerations: a hot site is fully equipped and current, offering fast recovery at high cost. A warm site has hardware but needs current data and setup. A cold site has space and utilities only. Environmental factors mean a recovery site should not share the same flood plain, power grid or earthquake zone.
Platform diversity reduces common-mode failure through a different vendor platform, different hardware or different virtualization technology.

Redundancy strategies: load balancing spreads requests across servers. Clustering groups servers so that one can take over from another. Autoscaling adds or removes capacity automatically. High availability means designing to minimize downtime. Multicloud systems use multiple providers. Storage redundancy includes RAID and replication. Power protection includes an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) for short-term battery power, a redundant power supply (RPS) in a device, a power generator for long outages and a surge protector for voltage spikes.
terms: A recovery site with only basic space and utilities.
Physical factors at a site such as flood risk.
Using different suppliers to avoid shared flaws.
Physical equipment choices that add diversity.
Software-based compute platforms, which can also be varied.
Grouping servers so that they can act together or fail over.
Uninterruptible power supply: short-term battery power.
Redundant power supply: a second supply in a device.
A machine that supplies sustained power.
A device that absorbs voltage spikes.
Disk systems, which can use RAID and replication for redundancy.
eg: A data centre rides through a brief outage on UPS while its generators start.
An online shop's load balancer stops sending traffic to a failed server, and customers do not notice.

table.caption: Power protection
rows: Second power supply inside a device

walks.title: Plan power for a server room
steps: Add a UPS sized to bridge the gap until the generator starts.
Add a generator for long outages, with fuel and testing.
Use dual power supplies connected to separate circuits.
Test it, because untested power protection is only a hope.

labs.title: Choose a recovery strategy
do: For three fictional organizations (a hospital, a small blog, a regional bank), choose a recovery site type.
Choose two redundancy strategies for each.
Estimate relative cost, and state what each organization is accepting.
labs.expect: Matching site choices to criticality, such as hot for the hospital and cold or cloud restore for the blog.
labs.explain: Spending should be proportional to the cost of downtime.
pass: Each organization has a site type with a reason.
Each organization has two redundancy strategies.

qs.s: Which site offers the fastest recovery?

a.w: It is fully equipped and current.

qs.s: Which device keeps equipment running briefly during an outage?

a.w: This is a cloud security tool.

qs.s: What is the main role of a load balancer?

a.w: That is an email security function.

qs.s: Why should a recovery site not be located close to the main site?

a.t: A regional event could affect both
a.w: Shared environmental risk defeats the purpose.

a.t: Data cannot be transmitted across short distances
Warm sites must be in another country by law
a.w: There is no such general rule.

a.t: It would reduce the backup's integrity

mistakes: Confusing UPS with a generator. A UPS bridges briefly, and a generator sustains longer.
Confusing redundancy with backup. Redundancy keeps things running, and backups restore lost data.
sum: Site type trades cost for recovery speed.
Redundancy removes single points of failure.
cards: Hot, warm or cold: which has only space and utilities?
What is the difference between a UPS and a generator?
A UPS bridges short outages, and a generator provides sustained power.
lessons.title: Resilience: sites, platform diversity, redundancy and power
lessons.why: Availability is one-third of the CIA triad. Ransomware, storms and hardware failure all test whether a business can keep working.
lessons.scenario: A business needs to resume in about two days after a disaster and wants moderate cost. Its equipment can be pre-installed, but data would need restoring. Which site fits?
lessons.answer: A warm site. It has equipment in place but needs current data and setup, with cost and recovery time between hot and cold.

product: Resilience appears as status pages, read-only modes and regional failover. Redundancy decisions determine whether a user experiences a moment of slowness or an afternoon offline.

eng: What do users experience during a failover?
sec: Does the secondary site keep the same security controls?
prod: What uptime have we committed to contractually?

design.noex: The failure-state exercise in Week 8 and the incident lesson cover the design work.

out: Design a backup approach that resists ransomware.
Define and calculate RTO, RPO, MTTR and MTBF.
Distinguish disaster recovery, business continuity and testing types.
plain: RPO is how far back you can afford to go: if the last save was four hours ago, you lose four hours of work. RTO is how long you can afford to be down. MTBF is how long something tends to work before breaking, and MTTR is how long it takes to fix.
tech: Backups involve retention (how long copies are kept), immutability (copies cannot be altered or deleted for a period, which resists ransomware), scope (what is included, such as full, incremental or differential) and restoration testing (proving a backup can be recovered). A common guideline is three copies, on two media, with one offsite.

Testing types: failover moves work to a standby system. Simulation walks through a scenario without affecting production. Parallel processing runs recovery systems alongside production to compare results. Disaster recovery focuses on restoring technology after a major event. Business continuity keeps the critical functions of the organization running. Capacity planning ensures that people, technology and infrastructure can meet expected demand.

Recovery metrics: the recovery time objective (RTO) is the maximum acceptable time to restore a service. The recovery point objective (RPO) is the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time. Mean time to repair (MTTR) is the average time to fix a failure. Mean time between failures (MTBF) is the average operating time between failures. MTBF equals total operating time divided by the number of failures.
terms: Copies of data kept for recovery.
How long backup copies are kept.
Backups that cannot be altered for a set period.
Proving that backups can be recovered.
Moving work to a standby system.
Practising a scenario without affecting production.
Running recovery systems alongside production to compare results.
Restoring technology after a major event.
Keeping critical functions running during disruption.
Making sure resources can meet expected demand.
Recovery time objective: maximum acceptable downtime.
Recovery point objective: maximum acceptable data loss, in time.
Mean time to repair: the average time to fix a failure.
Mean time between failures: average operating time between failures.
eg: Ransomware encrypts file servers, but immutable backups cannot be changed, so the business restores from them without paying.
A team discovers its backup job has been failing for months, the first time it attempts a restoration test.

table.caption: Recovery metrics
rows: How much data can we lose?
Backups every 4 hours give an RPO of up to 4 hours
How long can we be down?
How long does a repair take on average?
3 repairs took 6 hours in total, so 2 hours
How long between failures on average?

walks.title: Work out recovery metrics
steps: A database is backed up every 6 hours, so the RPO cannot be better than 6 hours.
A required restore takes 3 hours, plus 1 hour of checks, so RTO must be at least 4 hours.
A server ran 2,000 hours and failed 5 times, so MTBF is 400 hours.
Those 5 repairs took 10 hours in total, so MTTR is 2 hours.

labs.title: Back up and actually restore
do: Create a folder with five text files in your VM.
Run tar -czf backup.tar.gz myfolder and record the time.
Delete one file, and change another.
Restore into a new folder with mkdir restore, then tar -xzf backup.tar.gz -C restore, and confirm the original contents using diff.
State the RPO your backup represents.
labs.expect: The restored copy matches the state at the time of backup, and later edits are lost.
labs.explain: The difference between the backup time and the failure time is exactly what RPO measures.
pass: You restored and verified the files.

qs.s: Which metric describes the maximum acceptable data loss?

a.w: It is measured back in time from the failure.

qs.s: A device operated for 3,000 hours and failed 6 times. What is its MTBF?

a.w: This is the number of failures.
The values should be divided, not added.
The values should be divided, not multiplied.

qs.s: Which backup property best protects against ransomware that deletes backups?

a.w: Immutable copies cannot be changed or deleted during the lock period.
Backing up more does not protect the copies.

qs.s: A team brings the recovery system online alongside production and compares results, without moving users. What is this?

a.w: Both systems run together for comparison.
A simulation does not bring up real systems.

qs.s: Match each statement to its metric.
pairs: Lose no more than 15 minutes of data
qs.why: Time to restore, data lost, repair duration and failure frequency measure different things.

mistakes: Swapping RTO and RPO. Time points to downtime, and point refers to a point in the data.
Assuming a backup is good because the job reported success.
sum: Back up, keep an immutable copy and test restores.
RTO limits downtime, and RPO limits data loss.
MTBF measures reliability, and MTTR measures repair speed.
cards: RTO or RPO: maximum acceptable downtime?
Total operating time divided by the number of failures.
lessons.title: Backups, testing, disaster recovery and recovery metrics
lessons.why: A backup that has never been restored is an assumption. Recovery metrics turn vague hopes into commitments that a business can plan and pay for.
lessons.scenario: A company backs up at midnight every day. A failure occurs at 18:00 and the service is restored at 21:00. How much data was lost at most, and how long was the outage? Which metrics do these correspond to?
lessons.answer: Up to 18 hours of data were lost, which relates to RPO. The outage was 3 hours, which relates to RTO. If the business needs an RPO of four hours, daily backups will not meet it.

product: Recovery point objectives become product truth. If backups run hourly, a restore can lose up to an hour of work, and the interface and support team must say so honestly. Restore tools also need guarding, because a restore can erase current data.

eng: What are our actual recovery time and recovery point objectives?
sec: Are backups protected from an attacker who compromises production?
prod: Can customers restore their own data, and should they be able to?
